ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, on the left side there is a vertical wall, and at the bottom there is horizontal ground; at the same position on the lower right there is a person shooting a basketball. The figure shows two parabolic trajectories moving from the lower right toward the wall on the left, labeled 1 and 2 respectively. The impact point of trajectory 1 on the wall is obviously higher than the impact point of trajectory 2 on the wall. Reasoning: The problem states that in both cases the basketball strikes the vertical wall perpendicularly. The normal direction of a vertical wall is the horizontal direction, so at the instant the basketball strikes the wall, the direction of its velocity is horizontal, and its vertical component of velocity is 0. For oblique projectile motion, the position where the vertical component of velocity is 0 is the highest point of the trajectory, so the two wall-striking points are respectively the highest points of their own trajectories. Also because the two throws are made from the same position, and the highest point of trajectory 1 in the figure is higher than the highest point of trajectory 2, this indicates that the vertical component of the initial velocity in the 1st throw is larger. The time to rise to the highest point is t = v_{0y}/g; the larger the vertical initial velocity, the longer the time used to reach the highest point. Therefore, the time from being thrown to striking the wall is longer for the 1st throw and shorter for the 2nd throw.
